<description>
{
 "summary": "This pull request assigns mapped autonomous systems a distinct network group tag to prevent address group collisions with unmapped IPv6 /32 prefixes. It updates the peer bucketing format version so ASMap nodes rebucket stored addresses across upgrades and downgrades. Additionally, it fixes an issue where digit-leading filenames passed to `-asmap` were treated as boolean true, prevents `exportasmap` from overwriting existing files, and refines startup error handling for invalid map paths.",
 "problem": "Mapped AS numbers currently share the IPv6 group tag, causing nodes to conflate mapped autonomous systems with unmapped IPv6 /32 subnets and treat unrelated peers as belonging to the same address group when selecting connections or bucketing peers. In addition, setting `-asmap` to a filename starting with digits (such as `2026-09-asmap.dat`) caused argument parsing to interpret it as a boolean, silently using the embedded map instead of loading the user's file. Finally, `exportasmap` could silently overwrite an existing custom map on disk.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description: 'A mapped autonomous system and an unmapped IPv6 /32 can share an address group, so the node treats unrelated peers as part of the same network when selecting connections.'",
  "PR description and commit 81a507ab75: 'Reading `-asmap` as a boolean made a filename such as `2026-09-asmap.dat` select the embedded map.'",
  "Commit 119cf8b050: 'With `-asmap=asmap.dat`, running `exportasmap asmap.dat` replaces the configured map on disk with the embedded one. The running node keeps using the custom map until its next restart.'"
 ],

<category name="p2p" title="P2P">
## Covers

Everything between this node and other nodes: connection management and
peer selection, address management, the message protocol and its
transport (including the encrypted v2 transport), block and transaction
relay including compact blocks, headers sync, transaction request and
orphan handling, network-level DoS protections, and the Tor, I2P, and
CJDNS integrations. The P2P and Private Broadcast labels are a strong
prior.

Not p2p: what the node does with a block or transaction once received
(validation, mempool); RPCs that merely report peer state (rpc).

## What matters here

Resistance to attack first: eclipse and partition resistance, DoS
resistance in message handling and resource accounting, and privacy of
transaction origin. Then relay correctness and liveness: blocks and
transactions propagate reliably and quickly, and nothing gets stuck.
Then interoperability with the rest of the network and with new
protocol features (BIPs) that other software depends on. Then bandwidth
and resource use, which node operators feel. Then connectivity across
network types and platforms.

Protocol changes with a specification and other implementations
waiting rank higher than local optimizations. Refactors count when they
retire a known hazard in message handling.
